title: How land and climate shape life across India
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 4 'Different Lands, Different Lives' (plains, deserts, coasts and mountains: how land shapes food, clothes, houses, festivals, plants and animals) and Cambridge Stage 4 Unit 4.4 'Different habitats' (planet Earth and ecosystems: how animals are suited to their habitats). No textbook needed.
summary: India has snowy mountains, wide river plains, a hot sandy desert, a cold desert and long coasts. Each place has its own land and weather, and these decide which plants, animals and ways of life fit there. Your child makes a map of India they can touch, watches a tray 'river' build a plain, tests which pretend leaf keeps its water longest, and makes rain under a cold plate. They find out that a desert is any place with very little rain, so cold Ladakh is a desert too. They see how people in each place have adapted their food, clothes, houses and festivals. They learn how the monsoon brings rain from the sea and how the Himalaya were pushed up from the sea floor. Last, they argue both sides of bringing cheetahs back to India.
builds_on: Class 1: every place is somebody's home. Class 2: habitats, and how cactus, lotus, fish and camel fit their homes. Class 3: one tree and its soil, shared by animals of the day and of the night. Next: Class 5 explores India's unique places (Western Ghats, Sundarbans, Northeast, islands), endemic species, how natural selection builds adaptations, and how predators and prey shape each other.
goals: By the end your child can name India's main landforms and find each one on a map.
By the end your child can explain how the land and climate of a plain, a hot desert, a cold desert, a coast and a mountain shape the plants and animals there.
By the end your child can give examples of how people in each landform have adapted their food, clothes, houses and festivals.
By the end your child can explain that a desert is a place with very little rain, and why Ladakh is a desert.
By the end your child can describe how the monsoon forms and how the Himalaya were pushed up from the sea floor.
By the end your child can argue both sides of whether people should move animals, like cheetahs, to new habitats.
words: landform
a natural shape of the land: a plain, plateau, desert, coast, mountain or island
climate
the usual weather of a place over many years
plain
a wide, flat stretch of land, often made by rivers
plateau
high land with a fairly flat top, like the Deccan plateau
delta
the flat land a river builds out of silt where it meets the sea, like the Kaveri delta
silt
very fine soil that rivers carry and drop. It makes land fertile.
fertile
able to grow many plants well
cold desert
a desert that is cold, like Ladakh. Any place with very little rain or snow is a desert.
coast
where the land meets the sea
mangrove
a tree that grows in salty mud at the edge of the sea
condense
to turn from water vapour, an invisible gas, back into drops of water
rain shadow
the dry side of a range of hills, away from the sea, where little rain falls
monsoon
the season when winds from the sea bring heavy rain to India
altitude
how high a place is above the sea
ecosystem
all the living things in a place together with their land, water and air, all affecting each other
adaptation
a feature of the body, or a way of living, that helps a living thing survive where they live
subconcepts: landforms: plains, plateaus, deserts, coasts, mountains, islands
climate is the usual weather over many years
an ecosystem: land, water, climate and living things affecting each other
plains and deltas: rivers carry silt and make fertile land
hot deserts: how plants, animals and people save water
cold deserts: a desert is about water, not heat
coasts: salt, tides, mangroves, fishing and cyclones
mountains: cold, thin air and steep slopes
people adapt by culture: food, clothes, houses and festivals
people adapt in their bodies too: high-altitude genes
the monsoon: wet winds from the sea, and the rain shadow
the moving Earth makes landforms: the Himalaya were once sea floor
moving animals to new habitats: the cheetah debate

days.title: A map of India you can touch
days.goal: Recall the tree from Class 3, then look at India's landforms and make a map you can touch.

steps.title: From one tree to a whole country
steps.do: Ask: 'In Class 3 we watched one tree. Which animals used it by day? Which came at night? Who lived in the soil under it?' (By day: birds and squirrels. At night: owlets, bats and geckos. In the soil: earthworms and other decomposers, which make new soil.) Say: 'That was one tree. Now think of the whole of India. What would you see if you flew over it in a plane?' Let your child guess: mountains, rivers, sand, sea.

steps.title: Holiday postcards
steps.do: Ask: 'If you could go anywhere in India for a holiday, where would you go? What would you see, eat and wear there?' Write down answers for five places. A plain: the Kaveri delta around Thanjavur, or Punjab. A plateau: Hyderabad or Bengaluru on the Deccan. A desert: Jaisalmer or Ladakh. A coast: Kochi, Chennai or Puri. Mountains: the Nilgiris, Munnar or Sikkim. Ask: 'Why do you think people there eat different food and wear different clothes from us?' Keep the answers. You will check them through the week.

steps.title: Salt-dough relief map
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Trace an outline of India from an atlas onto a big piece of cardboard. Make the salt dough. Your child presses it onto the map to show the shape of the land. Make the Himalaya high and ridged across the top. Make the plains of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra low and flat below them. Make the Deccan plateau a raised table in the middle, with the hills of the Western and Eastern Ghats along its two sides. Leave flat strips for the coasts. Mark the Thar Desert in the northwest and Ladakh in the far north. Leave it to dry under a fan. You will paint it on Day 2.

steps.title: Say the landforms
steps.do: Your child runs a finger over the map and names each landform as they touch it: mountains, plains, plateau, desert, coast. Ask: 'Where do you think most rain falls? Where do most people live? Why?' (The most rain falls on the Western Ghats and in the Northeast. Most people live on the flat, fertile plains, where farming is easiest.)

need: an atlas or a printed map of India
2 cups atta or maida, 1 cup salt, about 3/4 cup water

days.title: Plains: the gift of the rivers
days.goal: See how rivers make plains and how plains feed most of India.

steps.title: A river makes a plain
steps.do: Do Experiment e1 in the bathroom or on the balcony. Build a slope of soil in a tray. First ask: 'If I pour water at the top, where will the soil end up? Why do you think so?' Then pour water slowly at the top to make a 'river'. Watch it cut a channel, carry mud, and drop it in a fan at the bottom. Your child feels the fine silt at the bottom. Ask: 'Why would farmers want to live where a river drops its silt?'

steps.title: Life on the plains
steps.do: Ask: 'In our tray, the river carried soil down the slope. Where do real rivers get their soil?' (From the mountains and hills they flow down.) Explain: the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra carry silt down from the Himalaya. In the south, the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri start in the Western Ghats and carry silt across the Deccan to their deltas on the east coast. For thousands of years, monsoon floods spread this silt over the flat land, so the plains and deltas became fertile. Ask: 'What grows there?' (Rice, wheat, sugarcane, bananas, mustard and vegetables.) 'Which festivals celebrate the harvest?' (Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Onam in Kerala, Sankranti in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka, Baisakhi in Punjab, Bihu in Assam.) Ask: 'Why are so many festivals about the harvest?' Then ask: 'The same river that brings silt also floods homes. Is a flood good or bad for a farmer? Can it be both?'

steps.title: Paint the map
steps.do: Paint the dried map: white for snow, brown and grey for mountains, green for the fertile plains, yellow-orange for the Thar, pale grey-brown for the cold desert of Ladakh, dark green for the forests of the Ghats and the Northeast, blue for the rivers and sea. Your child paints each river from the mountains down to the sea. Ask: 'Where does the soil of the plains come from?' (From the mountains. The rivers carried it down.)

steps.title: Postcard check
steps.do: Look at the Day 1 postcard answers for the plains. Were they right? Add one new thing your child now knows. Ask: 'If the Himalaya disappeared, what would happen to the northern plains?' (No new silt would come down. The big northern rivers would also carry much less water in summer, when melting snow fills them.)

need: a big tray or plastic sheet
soil from a plant pot, with a little sand if you have it

days.title: The hot desert: every drop counts
days.goal: Find out how plants, animals and people of the Thar live with very little water.

steps.title: Three leaves in the sun
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Make three pretend leaves from wet paper towels. Leave one flat and open. Roll one into a tight tube. Lay the third flat and cover the top with a piece of plastic bag, like a waxy coat. Ask: 'Which will stay wet longest? Why do you think so?' Put all three in the sun. Do the next step while you wait.

steps.title: Desert survival kit
steps.do: Ask: 'What is the hardest thing about living in the Thar?' (Rain comes only a few times a year, and the hot sun dries everything.) Then go through who lives there and how each one saves water. The khejri tree: their roots go very deep, down to water far under the sand. Thor, a spiny plant with a fat green stem: they store water in the stem and have almost no leaves to lose it from. Desert grasses: their seeds wait in the sand and sprout quickly after rain. The camel: their body loses very little water, their droppings are dry, and their body warms up by day instead of sweating. The desert fox and the desert cat: they rest in burrows and shade by day and hunt at night, when it is cool. The chinkara, a small gazelle: they can go a long time without drinking, because they get water from the plants they eat. People: loose, light-coloured clothes and turbans shade the body. Thick mud walls keep houses cool. Underground tanks called tankas catch every drop of rain. Foods like bajra, dried beans and ker-sangri keep for months without spoiling. Ask: 'What is the same about the camel, the khejri and the people?' (They all save water.)

steps.title: Read the leaves
steps.do: Check Experiment e2. Which towel stayed wet longest? Why? Explain: the rolled towel is like a leaf that rolls up. Paddy leaves roll into thin tubes at midday in a dry spell, and many desert grasses do the same. The covered towel is like the waxy skin of thor and cactus. Ask: 'If you were a desert plant, which would you choose?'

steps.title: Desert song and dance
steps.do: The Thar has rich folk music. Much of it is sung by Manganiyar and Langa families, who have been musicians for generations. Play a recording of a Manganiyar song if you can. Then your child makes up a desert dance in three parts. First, the long, still heat: slow, heavy movements. Then the sudden rain: fast, joyful spinning. Last, the land soaking up the water: sinking down slowly. Ask: 'Why might people in a desert celebrate rain more than people in Kerala do?'

days.title: The cold desert and the roof of the world
days.goal: Discover that Ladakh is a desert, and how life and people adapt high in the mountains.

steps.title: Story: Two Deserts
steps.do: Read the story 'Two Deserts' aloud. Don't explain it. Ask the story questions. Then ask: 'Why did Pooja think Dolkar had lots of water? Why was she wrong?'

steps.title: Ice that waits for spring
steps.do: Ask: 'Ladakh's farmers must sow barley in April and May. But their streams fill with glacier water only in June. What could they do?' Let your child think. Then tell them about voice v1, Chewang Norphel, an engineer from Ladakh. He builds 'artificial glaciers'. In winter, stream water is spread over a shady place near the village, where it freezes and stays frozen. In spring it melts, just when the farmers need it. Later, Sonam Wangchuk's team built ice stupas: tall cones of ice that melt slowly, because a cone has less surface facing the sun. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Mountain breath
steps.do: Ask: 'Why do people who fly to Leh feel out of breath for the first few days?' Explain: high up, the air is thinner, so each breath brings in less oxygen. Feel what happens when your body needs more oxygen. Sit still and count your breaths for 30 seconds. Then walk briskly up and down the stairs, or march on the spot, for one minute. Sit and count again. Then do mountain pose (tadasana): stand tall, feet together, arms by your sides, still as a mountain. Breathe slowly in for 4 counts and out for 4 counts, five times.

steps.title: Bodies that fit the mountains
steps.do: Ask: 'Can a body be built for thin air?' Tell your child about voice v2. Many Tibetan and Sherpa people, whose families have lived very high up for thousands of years, carry a version of a gene called EPAS1. It helps their bodies cope with thin air without making their blood too thick. This version probably came from the Denisovans, an ancient kind of human who lived in Asia and had children with our ancestors. Ask the voice question. Then talk about mountain animals and plants, each with their problem first. Cold: the yak has long, thick hair, and the snow leopard has thick fur and a long tail to wrap round their face. Thin air: the yak has big lungs. A winter with no fresh plants: the pika, a small furry animal, stores piles of dry grass. Heavy snow: deodar and pine trees have sloping branches, so the snow slides off. Steep cliffs: the Nilgiri tahr, a wild goat of the Nilgiris and Munnar, climbs rocky slopes where predators cannot follow.

steps.title: Desert or not?
steps.do: Ask: 'Is Ladakh a desert? Is Antarctica? Is Cherrapunji in Meghalaya?' (Ladakh: yes. Antarctica: yes, it is the biggest desert on Earth. Cherrapunji: no, it is one of the wettest places on Earth.) Ask: 'So what makes a place a desert?' (Very little rain or snow, not heat.) Look at the postcard answers for the mountains.

need: stairs or space to march on the spot

days.title: Coasts, and the monsoon's long journey
days.goal: See how life fits the salty, windy coast, and how the ocean and sky make the monsoon.

steps.title: Life where land meets sea
steps.do: Ask: 'What problems does a living thing face at the edge of the sea?' (Salty water and soil, strong winds, storms, and tides that come in and go out.) Then talk about how coast life copes. Coconut palms: their trunks bend in storms instead of snapping, and their nuts float to new beaches. Mangroves, like those at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu: they grow in salty mud, have roots that stick up out of the mud to breathe, and slow down waves. Animals: crabs, mudskippers (fish that walk on mud), and olive ridley turtles, who come to lay eggs on beaches in Odisha and Chennai. People: they catch fish, and in Kerala and Goa the food is full of fish, rice and coconut. Houses in rainy Kerala have steep tiled roofs so the heavy rain runs off. In Maharashtra, fisherfolk offer a coconut to the sea at Narali Purnima, when fishing starts again after the heaviest rains. Ask: 'Why is a coconut palm a good coast tree?'

steps.title: Make a monsoon
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. A grown-up handles the hot water. First ask: 'Where do you think rain comes from?' Steam rises from a bowl of hot water (the warm sea), meets a cold steel plate with ice on it (the cool air high up), and drips back down as 'rain'. Ask: 'Where did the rain on the plate come from?' (Water that evaporated from the bowl, just as water evaporates from the warm sea.) Explain: when wet sea air is pushed up a range of hills, it cools, like the steam at the cold plate, and drops its rain. Ask: 'Mangaluru is on the sea side of the Western Ghats. Bengaluru is on the other side. Which gets more rain?' (Mangaluru gets more than three times as much. Bengaluru is in the rain shadow.)

steps.title: Drama: Ocean and Sky
steps.do: Act out the monsoon. You play the Sea and your child plays the Land, then swap. Land: 'In May the sun heats me fast. The air above me gets hot and rises.' Sea: 'I warm up slowly, so the air over me stays cooler. It blows towards you to fill the space, and it carries water vapour from me.' Make a hill of cushions next to the Land. Your child becomes the wind and carries a cloud (a pillow) from the Sea up the hill. At the top the cloud cools, and they drop 'rain' (torn paper) on the sea side of the hill. Little is left for the far side: that is the rain shadow. Add people waiting for the rain: a farmer near Thanjavur, a fisherwoman in Kochi watching the clouds.

steps.title: When the sea gets angry
steps.do: Ask: 'What is a cyclone?' (A huge spinning storm that forms over warm sea.) Explain: the east coast, from Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh up to Odisha and Bengal, gets many cyclones. In 1999 a super cyclone killed about 10,000 people in Odisha. In 2013 Cyclone Phailin hit the same coast, but early warnings moved about a million people to shelters, and far fewer died. Ask: 'How could a mangrove forest also protect a village?' (Mangroves slow down the waves and the water the storm pushes onto the land.) Ask: 'What could protect people: sea walls, shelters, warnings, mangroves? Which of these is alive and grows by itself?'

steps.title: Coast postcard
steps.do: Check the coast postcard from Day 1 and add one thing your child now knows.

need: a heat-proof bowl of hot water
cushions, a pillow and some torn paper for the play

days.title: How the land itself was made
days.goal: See that landforms are made by a moving Earth, and meet the woman who mapped the sea floor.

steps.title: Push up a mountain
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Lay three towels of different colours flat on a table, one on top of another. They are layers of rock on the sea floor. Put a small shell or button on the top towel. Ask: 'What will happen if I push from both ends?' Push slowly from both ends towards the middle and watch the towels fold up into ridges. Explain: about 50 million years ago, the land that is now India was moving north across the ocean, and it began to push into Asia. It is still pushing, a few centimetres a year. The sea floor between them was squeezed and lifted up into the Himalaya. Ask: 'If the Himalaya were once sea floor, what might you find on top of them?'

steps.title: Seashells on the mountain
steps.do: Answer the question: fossils of sea animals are found high in the Himalaya. Many are ammonites, sea animals with curly shells who died out at the same time as the dinosaurs. Some black stones from the Gandaki river in Nepal, worshipped as shaligrams, hold ammonite fossils more than 100 million years old. Ask: 'How does a sea shell end up on top of a mountain?' Let your child explain it with the towels. Say: 'The ground under us is moving, slowly, all the time.'

steps.title: Marie Tharp maps the sea floor
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3, Marie Tharp. In the 1950s women were not allowed on the research ships, so she drew maps of the ocean floor from measurements other people took at sea. She found a deep crack running down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean floor, where the sea floor is splitting apart. Her colleague first dismissed it as 'girl talk'. Later her maps helped show that the Earth's surface moves, the same movement that pushed up the Himalaya. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Read each question aloud if needed. For the 'why' questions, ask your child to answer in a full sentence and to use one new word (silt, climate, altitude, adaptation).

steps.title: One sentence
steps.do: Your child finishes: 'The Himalaya are still growing because…' (India is still pushing into Asia).

need: 3 towels or sheets of different colours
a picture of an ammonite fossil or a shaligram if you can find one

days.title: Should we move animals to new homes?
days.goal: Argue a real debate about habitats, design a home for a landform and play the game.

steps.title: The cheetah debate
steps.do: Talk about voice v4. Cheetahs once lived in India, but they were hunted until none were left by about 1952. In 2022 and 2023, cheetahs from Namibia and South Africa were brought to Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh. Some have had cubs, and several have died. Hold a mini-debate. First your child argues FOR bringing cheetahs back: it returns an animal that people wiped out, and it may help protect grasslands. Then AGAINST: Kuno may be too small, the cheetahs came from different climates, leopards compete with them, and the money could protect animals already here. Then ask the voice question, and let your child give their own verdict with a reason.

steps.title: Design a home for a landform
steps.do: Your child chooses one landform and designs a house and an outfit for living there, with labels explaining each choice. Desert: thick mud walls, small windows, an underground tank, loose cotton clothes. Mountain: thick stone walls, a flat roof for drying apricots, wool, a stove in the middle. Rainy Kerala coast: a steep tiled roof with wide edges, a raised floor, light cotton. Plains: a courtyard, a verandah, a store for grain. Ask: 'Which of these choices do the same job as a camel's feet or a yak's hair, but were worked out by people instead of grown by a body?'

steps.title: Journey Across India board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1. On each landform square, a player must name one plant or animal and one human way of life that fit it.

need: the printed board, a die and counters

days.title: My own landform, and teach it back
days.goal: Study the landform around your own home and teach the whole topic back.

steps.title: Life in my landform
steps.do: Finish the project. Walk around your area, or look out from your balcony or window, and answer these. Is our land flat, hilly, coastal or dry? Where does our water come from (a river, a lake, a borewell, a tank, the city supply)? What trees and birds are common here? What do people here eat that is grown nearby? What are the houses made of, and why? Your child writes or draws one answer for each. Ask: 'How has our landform shaped our family's life without us noticing?'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Read each question aloud and talk about the written answers before your child writes them down.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child uses the relief map to give a five-minute 'tour of India' to the family: for each landform, one plant, one animal, one human adaptation. They must explain why Ladakh is a desert, how the monsoon forms, and how the Himalaya rose from the sea. Then ask the check questions. Keen thinkers can do Worksheet ws3 on another day.

sections.p: Match the landform to its description.
pairs: wide, flat land made by rivers
a place with very little rain
high land with a flat top

sections.p: The fine soil that rivers carry and drop on the plains is called ____.
Why do so many people in India live on the northern plains?
opts: the land is flat and fertile, with river water for farming
it gets the most rain in India

sections.p: Which landform does each living thing fit best?
Ladakh is a desert because…
opts: it gets very little rain or snow

sections.p: In Jaisalmer, a family's roof slopes so that rain runs into an underground tank. Why?
opts: the tank keeps the roof cool
rain is rare, so every drop is stored to drink all year

sections.p: Why do desert houses have thick mud walls and small windows?
How did sea fossils end up high in the Himalaya?
Most monsoon rain falls on the side of the Western Ghats that faces…
The monsoon rain comes from water that evaporated from…
People who travel to Ladakh feel out of breath because…
opts: there is less oxygen in each breath high up

sections.p: Match the human adaptation to the landform.
pairs: steep tiled roof with wide edges

sections.p: All the living things in a place together with their land, water and air are called an ____.
Is it about the land, the climate, or the living things?
The plains would slowly become less fertile if…
opts: the Himalaya stopped sending snow-fed rivers and silt

sections.p: A camel and a person in Jaisalmer both have ways to save water. Give one way for each.
Is a river flood a gift or a disaster for a farmer on the plains? Give a reason for each side.
The biggest desert in the world is…
Tibetan people cope with thin air partly because of a gene that probably came from…
opts: an ancient kind of human, the Denisovans

sections.p: A cone of ice (ice stupa) melts more slowly than a flat sheet of the same ice because…
opts: less of its surface faces the sun
it is made of salt water

sections.p: A dam is built across a river high above a plain. It stops the floods on the plain. What else might it stop?
Is it an adaptation made by evolution (in the body) or by culture (people's know-how)?
Should cheetahs have been brought to India? Give the strongest reason for, the strongest against, and your own view.
Some people say the Thar is a 'wasteland' that should be turned into farms or solar parks. Who lives there already? What might be lost?
Kavya says a camel is better adapted than a yak. Meena says that makes no sense. Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then answer back as the other girl.

experiments.title: A river makes a plain
experiments.question: How do rivers make flat, fertile plains?
need: a big tray or a plastic sheet with raised edges
soil from a plant pot, mixed with a little sand if you have some
a few books to prop up one end
a jug of water or a watering can
steps: Pile the soil in a slope at one end of the tray (the mountains), and prop that end up on books.
Leave the low end empty (the plain and the sea).
Pour water slowly onto the top of the slope for about a minute. Watch.
Pour again two or three times.
Look at the channel the water made, and at what has collected at the bottom.
Rub the bottom mud between your fingers.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Where will the soil end up? Will the slope change?'
experiments.observe: The water cuts a channel down the slope and carries soil with it. At the bottom, where the land flattens and the water slows, it drops the soil in a flat fan: coarse sand first, fine silky silt furthest out.
experiments.why: Fast water can carry soil, and slow water drops it. Rivers rushing down mountains pick up rock and soil. When they reach flat land they slow down and spread out, especially in floods, and leave their silt behind. Over thousands of years this builds deep, soft, fertile plains, like the plain of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. Where a river meets the sea, it builds a delta in the same way, like the Kaveri delta in Tamil Nadu and the Sundarbans in Bengal.
experiments.safety: Do it in the bathroom, on the balcony or outside, where the mud can be washed away.

experiments.title: Three leaves in the sun
experiments.question: Which leaf shape or coat saves the most water?
need: 3 paper towels of the same size
a piece of plastic bag the size of one towel
steps: Wet all three paper towels equally and squeeze out the drips.
Lay one flat and open on a plate.
Roll one into a tight tube and put it on the second plate.
Lay the third flat on a plate and cover the top with the plastic.
Put all three plates in the sun.
Every 15 minutes, touch each towel and say if it is wet, damp or dry. At the end, unroll the rolled one and feel the inside.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which one will stay wet longest? Why?'
experiments.observe: The flat, open towel dries first. The rolled one is still wet inside, and the covered one stays wet much longer.
experiments.why: Water escapes into the air from surfaces that touch the air. A flat, open leaf has a lot of surface in the sun and wind, so it loses water fast. Rolling hides most of the surface. That is why paddy leaves and many desert grasses roll up in dry heat. A waxy coat seals the surface, and desert plants such as thor and cactus have a thick one. Many desert plants also have tiny leaves or none, and open the tiny holes in their stems and leaves mostly at night, when it is cool.
experiments.time: 15 min to set up, then a quick check every 15 minutes for about 45 minutes

experiments.title: Make a monsoon
experiments.question: Where does monsoon rain come from?
need: a heat-proof glass or steel bowl
hot water (from a kettle, handled only by a grown-up)
steps: A grown-up pours hot (not boiling) water into the bowl.
Put ice cubes on the steel plate and hold it over the bowl, a little above it.
Wait 2–3 minutes.
Look at the underside of the plate. Tilt it a little.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen under the cold plate?'
experiments.observe: Steam rises, the underside of the plate fogs up, drops form and grow, and they drip back down like rain.
experiments.why: Warm water evaporates into invisible water vapour. When the vapour meets something cold, it condenses into drops. In early summer the land of India heats up faster than the ocean. Hot air over the land rises, and moist air from the warm Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal flows in to replace it. When this wet air is pushed up over the Western Ghats or the hills of the Northeast, it cools and drops huge amounts of rain. The side of the hills away from the sea gets far less: a 'rain shadow'. The monsoon links the ocean, the air, the land and every farm in India: what happens in a far-off ocean can change whether your town gets rain.
experiments.safety: Only a grown-up handles the hot water. Use hot, not boiling, water and keep faces away from the steam.

activities.title: Salt-dough relief map of India
need: salt dough (2 cups atta or maida, 1 cup salt, about 3/4 cup water)
steps: Trace or draw India's outline on the cardboard.
Mix the salt dough until it is like soft clay.
Build the Himalaya high and ridged across the top, the plains low and flat below them, the Deccan plateau raised in the middle, the Ghats as low hills along both sides, flat coasts all round.
Mark the Thar Desert and Ladakh.
Let it dry for a day, then paint it (Day 2) and label the landforms and big rivers.
activities.outcome: A painted, labelled 3D map of India's landforms to use all week.

activities.title: Push up a mountain
need: 3 towels or sheets of paper of different colours
steps: Lay the three towels flat, one on top of the other, like layers of rock on the sea floor.
Put a small shell or button on the top layer (a sea creature).
Push slowly from both ends towards the middle.
Watch the layers fold and rise.
Find where the shell has ended up.
activities.outcome: A model showing how India pushing into Asia folded the sea floor up into the Himalaya, carrying sea fossils with it.

project.title: Life in my landform
steps: Find out what landform you live on: plain, plateau, coast, hills, desert.
Find out where your water comes from.
List five plants and five animals common in your area.
Find three foods grown near you and one local festival linked to the land or the seasons.
Look at local houses: what are they made of? Why?
Make a one-page poster: 'How our land shapes our life'.
project.outcome: A poster showing how the land, water and climate around your home shape its plants, animals and people, including your own family.

game.title: Journey Across India
rules: Start at the Himalaya and travel to the sea. Roll the die and move.
On a landform square (MOUNTAIN, PLAIN, DESERT, COLD DESERT, COAST, PLATEAU), name one plant or animal AND one human adaptation that fit it. If the others agree, move forward 1.
On an event square, follow what it says.
No one can repeat an answer already given in the game.
First to reach THE SEA wins, and must say how the water in the sea might come back to the Himalaya (evaporation, monsoon, snow).
squares: Landslide on a bare slope: back 2
You built an artificial glacier: forward 2
River dried by too much pumping: back 2
You found a tanka full of rainwater: forward 2
Mangroves cut down for shrimp ponds: back 3

big: Does the land shape people more, or do people shape the land more?
If you were born in Ladakh, would you be the same person you are now?
Is a desert empty, or full of a different kind of life?
Our rain is water that evaporated from the sea. If a far-away ocean warms up, could it change the rain in your town?
Should people bring back animals that people made extinct? Who should decide?

challenge.q: Many people think deserts are hot, sandy places. Is that what makes a desert?
challenge.hint: A desert is any place with very little rain or snow. Leh in Ladakh gets about 100 mm of rain and snow in a year, less than Jaisalmer in the Thar (roughly 150–200 mm). Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth. What problem do all deserts share?

challenge.q: People often say the Himalaya are 'eternal', the oldest, most unchanging mountains. True?
challenge.hint: The Himalaya are among the YOUNGEST big mountains on Earth, and still rising, by a few millimetres a year, as India keeps pushing into Asia. The Aravalli hills in Rajasthan are far older, worn down over hundreds of millions of years. Why do you think we think of mountains as never changing?

challenge.q: We hear that mangroves are 'useless swamps'. Are they?
challenge.hint: Mangroves are nurseries for young fish and crabs, homes for birds and, in the Sundarbans, tigers, and they store a lot of carbon in their mud. Studies after the 2004 tsunami at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu and the 1999 Odisha cyclone suggest that villages behind mangroves suffered less damage. Scientists still argue about how much. Useless to whom?

perspectives.view: In Ladakh, villages share the meltwater from glaciers through channels, and a village water-keeper (often called the churpon) decides whose fields get water when. Ask: is water something a person can own? How should a village share something that everyone needs?

She reads the sea and sky every morning: the colour of the water, the wind, the birds. Her family has done this for generations. Ask: how is her knowledge like a weather scientist's? How is it different? Could they help each other?

If the Ganga could speak, she might say: 'Every monsoon I carry soil from the mountains and spread it over the plains. That soil feeds you. You built towns on the land where I used to spread out, and now you call my floods disasters.' Ask: who was there first? What would the river want?

She lives on cliffs above 3,000 metres, where her prey, blue sheep and ibex, also live. As the climate warms, the tree line and common leopards are moving higher up some mountains. Ask: where can a snow leopard go when there is no higher ground left?

voices.who: Chewang Norphel, civil engineer, Ladakh, India (the 'Ice Man')
voices.idea: Ladakh's farmers need water in April and May to sow barley, but the high glaciers melt only in June. Norphel noticed that water left trickling in shady places froze in winter and stayed frozen. From 1987 he built 'artificial glaciers': he diverted winter streams into shaded, stepped stone walls so that the water froze in layers close to the villages, and melted in spring, just when it was needed. Later, the engineer and educator Sonam Wangchuk and his team built tall cones of ice called ice stupas, which melt more slowly because a cone has less surface facing the sun.
voices.then: At first, some people doubted that small homemade glaciers could make a real difference. Villagers who saw their fields watered in spring changed their minds.
voices.now: His artificial glaciers have watered fields in many Ladakhi villages, and he received the Padma Shri in 2015. Scientists agree they help locally. They cannot replace real glaciers, which are shrinking as the climate warms.
voices.ask: Norphel used a simple observation: shade keeps ice frozen. What simple thing near your home could be used to save water?

voices.who: Cynthia Beall, anthropologist, USA, and Emilia Huerta-Sánchez, Rasmus Nielsen and colleagues (2014)
voices.idea: For decades Cynthia Beall studied people who live high in the Tibetan Plateau, the Andes and Ethiopia, and found they cope with thin air in different ways: many Andean highlanders have more red blood cells, while many Tibetans breathe faster and keep their blood thinner. In 2010 several teams found that a gene called EPAS1 had changed in Tibetans. In 2014 Huerta-Sánchez, Nielsen and colleagues showed that the Tibetan version of EPAS1 probably came from the Denisovans, an ancient group of humans who had children with the ancestors of Tibetans long ago.
voices.then: Many people had assumed all humans adapt to high altitude in the same way, simply by making more blood. The idea that a gene from another kind of ancient human helps people today surprised many.
voices.now: Accepted. It is one of the clearest examples of humans adapting to a habitat in their bodies, not only through clothes and houses. It also shows that human history is a story of different peoples meeting and mixing.
voices.ask: The people of Tibet adapted with their bodies over thousands of years, and also with yak-wool clothes and stone houses. Which kind of adaptation is faster? Which is easier to share with others?

voices.idea: In the 1950s, women were not allowed on the research ships, so Tharp worked on land, drawing maps of the sea floor by hand from depth measurements collected at sea. In 1952 she found a deep valley running down the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a rift where the sea floor is splitting apart. With her colleague Bruce Heezen she later made the first map of the whole world's ocean floor (1977).
voices.then: When she first showed Heezen the rift, he dismissed it as 'girl talk', partly because it supported continental drift, an idea most geologists then rejected. More data proved her right, and he came round, but for decades her role was often credited to him.
voices.now: Her maps helped convince scientists that the Earth's surface is broken into moving plates, the same movement that pushed up the Himalaya. She is now honoured as one of the great mapmakers of the planet.
voices.ask: Tharp was right, but she was not allowed on the ships and her idea was laughed at. Who else might have had good ideas that were never written down because they weren't allowed in the room?

voices.who: Project Cheetah (2022 onwards) and its critics, India
voices.idea: The cheetah was hunted to extinction in India by about 1952. In September 2022, eight cheetahs from Namibia were released into Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh, followed by twelve from South Africa in 2023. Supporters, including the government and some wildlife scientists, said bringing back a lost top predator would help protect India's neglected grasslands and the animals in them.
voices.then: Several Indian ecologists, including Ravi Chellam, argued that Kuno is too small for wide-ranging cheetahs, has leopards that compete with them, and that the money might do more good protecting animals already here, such as the great Indian bustard. Kuno had first been prepared for Asiatic lions from Gir, which have still not been moved there.
voices.now: Some cheetahs have survived and had cubs born in India. Several adults and cubs have died, from causes including heat, fights and infections. Whether the project can create a lasting wild population is still argued.
voices.ask: What would you need to see in ten years' time to say the cheetahs belong in India again?

story.title: Two Deserts
text: Dolkar had never seen so much sand.

It went on and on outside the bus window, gold and rippled like the skin on hot milk, all the way to the edge of the sky. Here and there a thorny tree stood alone, holding up a little round of shade like an umbrella. A line of camels walked along the horizon, slow and proud, as if they were thinking about something important.

"Welcome to the desert!" said her cousin Pooja, when the bus finally stopped in Jaisalmer and she ran to hug her. "Poor you. You must be dying in this heat. Up in Ladakh you've got snow and glaciers and rivers. You've got so much water there."

Dolkar opened her mouth to answer, and then closed it again, because the heat had climbed inside it. She had come from a place where, in January, the water in the bucket outside the door froze solid overnight. Here the air pressed on her like a hand.

Pooja's house had walls as thick as Dolkar's arm was long, made of yellow stone and mud, with tiny windows. Inside it was dim and almost cool. Pooja's mother poured water for them from a clay pot, very carefully, so that not one drop fell on the floor. Dolkar noticed that. She noticed that the leftover water from washing vegetables was poured onto the little tulsi in the courtyard. She noticed that in the middle of the courtyard there was a round stone lid, like a giant coin.
"What's that?" she asked.
"Our tanka," said Pooja. "It's a tank under the ground. When it rains, the roof and the courtyard are sloped so every drop runs into it. Then we drink it all year."
"How often does it rain?"
Pooja shrugged. "Not much. A few times, in the monsoon. Some years hardly at all." She looked at Dolkar with a little bit of envy. "You're lucky. You don't have to worry about water."
That night, on the flat roof, under more stars than Dolkar had ever seen except at home, she told Pooja the truth.
"It hardly ever rains in Ladakh either," she said. "Hardly ever snows in the valleys. My teacher says we get less rain than you do here."
Pooja sat up. "That's not possible. You live in the mountains. In the snow."
"The snow is high up, on the mountains, far away," said Dolkar. "Down in our village it's dry. Dry like here, only cold. The mountains all around stop the clouds. We're a desert, too. A cold one."
Pooja was quiet for a long time. A camel groaned somewhere below them.
"Then where does your water come from?"

So Dolkar told her. She told her about the glaciers that sit high on the mountains like white hats, and how they melt in summer and send water rushing down the streams. She told her about the little channels her father and the neighbours dug and cleaned together every spring, and the old man in the village whose job it was to decide whose fields got the water each day, so it was fair. She told her about the problem: the glaciers melted in June, but the barley had to be sown in April, when the streams were still frozen and silent.
"So what do you do?" asked Pooja.
Dolkar grinned in the dark. "We make our own glaciers."

She explained how, in winter, the people in her village led a stream into a shady valley near the fields, where the sun hardly reached, and let it spread out over little stone walls. Night after night it froze, layer on layer, into a long white sheet of ice. Then, in spring, when the sun climbed higher, the ice slowly melted, just in time, right next to the fields. "A man called Norphel thought of it," she said. "He noticed that water in the shade stays frozen. Now some villages make ice towers, too, tall ones, like stupas. A tall shape melts slower."
Pooja was staring at her. "You save the winter," she said slowly, "for the spring."
"Yes."
"And we save the monsoon," said Pooja, and she pointed down at the round stone lid in the courtyard, "for the whole year."

They looked at each other. Dolkar's breath came out in a long, surprised laugh, and Pooja laughed too, and for a moment the two deserts, the hot gold one and the cold brown one, two thousand kilometres apart, felt like the same place.

On the last day of her visit, Dolkar unpacked the present she had carried all the way from Leh: a bag of apricots, dried hard and sweet on the flat roof of her house in the autumn sun. Pooja gave her a bag of ker berries and sangri beans, dried in the Thar sun, which her mother said would keep for a year.

On the long bus ride home, Dolkar held the bag on her lap and thought about the tanka, and the thick walls, and the careful clay pot. When she got back to her village, the first thing she did was help her mother carry water from the stream. She didn't spill a drop.
story.epiphany: A desert is defined by water, not heat: both the hot Thar and cold Ladakh get very little rain (Leh even less than Jaisalmer), so plants, animals and people in both have adapted to save and store water, in time (artificial glaciers save winter for spring) and in space (tankas save the monsoon for the year). The turn is Dolkar's 'We're a desert, too', and Pooja's realisation that both families do the same thing in opposite ways. Landforms and climate shape culture: houses, food, sharing rules. The artificial glaciers of Chewang Norphel are real. The girls are invented.
ask: Why did Pooja think Dolkar had lots of water? Why was she wrong?
What makes a place a desert?
How does Pooja's family save water? How does Dolkar's village?
What did Pooja mean by 'You save the winter for the spring'?
Why do you think both families dry their food on the roof?

ideas.idea: The land and its weather shape everything that lives on it, including us.
ideas.more: Rivers make fertile plains, where most people live. Little rain shaped the camel, the khejri and the tanka. Thin air shaped the yak, and even the genes of Tibetan people. Our food, clothes, houses and festivals are adaptations too, worked out by people instead of grown by bodies.

ideas.idea: A desert is about water, not heat.
ideas.more: Ladakh and Antarctica are deserts. All deserts share one problem: very little water. Life in all of them has found ways to catch, store and save it.

ideas.idea: The ground moves, and the sea brings our rain.
ideas.more: The Himalaya were pushed up from the sea floor and are still rising. Monsoon rain is water that evaporated from the warm sea and was carried to the land by the wind.

unknowns: How will shrinking Himalayan glaciers change the rivers of the plains, and the lives of hundreds of millions of people downstream? Scientists are still working out how much, and how fast.
Nobody can yet predict reliably, months ahead, whether a monsoon will be strong or weak. Links to faraway oceans, like El Niño in the Pacific, help, but are not the whole story.
Will the cheetahs in Kuno become a lasting wild population? It will take many years to know.
How many genes from ancient humans like the Denisovans help people in other habitats today? Scientists are still finding new ones.

books.title: One Well: The Story of Water on Earth
books.author: Rochelle Strauss
books.why: All the water on Earth as one shared well: how it moves through seas, skies, plants, animals and us, and why it must be shared.

books.title: The Water Princess
books.author: Susan Verde (based on the childhood of Georgie Badiel)
books.why: A girl in Burkina Faso walks every day to fetch water. A moving look at life where water is scarce, like the Thar.

books.title: Solving the Puzzle Under the Sea: Marie Tharp Maps the Ocean Floor
books.author: Robert Burleigh
books.why: Marie Tharp's life and maps, and how a woman kept off the ships changed what we know about the moving Earth.

books.title: Where the Forest Meets the Sea
books.author: Jeannie Baker
books.why: A boy explores a rainforest on the coast of Australia, in astonishing collage pictures, and wonders what will happen to it.

books.title: Ancient Futures: Learning from Ladakh
books.author: Helena Norberg-Hodge
books.age: adult (read the chapters on farming and water-sharing aloud)
books.why: How Ladakhi villages lived well for centuries in a cold desert by sharing water and land, and what changed when the modern economy arrived.

check.q: Name India's main landforms and one place for each.
check.a: Mountains: the Himalaya and the Western Ghats. Plains: the Kaveri delta, Punjab, Bihar and Bengal. Plateau: the Deccan, with Hyderabad and Bengaluru. Hot desert: the Thar. Cold desert: Ladakh. Coasts: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Goa and Odisha. Islands: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.

check.q: Why are the northern plains so fertile?
check.a: Rivers from the Himalaya carry silt and spread it over the plains, especially in floods, over thousands of years.

check.q: What makes a place a desert? Why is Ladakh one?
check.a: Very little rain or snow. Ladakh is a cold desert. The mountains around it block the rain clouds, so Leh gets even less rain than Jaisalmer.

check.q: Give one adaptation of a plant, an animal and people in the hot desert.
check.a: Plant: the khejri's deep roots, or the waxy skin of thor. Animal: the camel's dry droppings, or the desert fox hunting at night. People: tankas, thick mud walls, loose light clothes.

check.q: How does the monsoon bring rain?
check.a: The land heats up in summer. Moist air from the warm sea flows in, rises over hills, cools and drops its water as rain.
India moved north and pushed into Asia, folding and lifting the sea floor between them. It is still pushing, so the Himalaya are still rising. That is why sea fossils are found on them.

check.q: Give one reason for and one against bringing cheetahs to India.
check.a: For: restoring a lost predator and protecting grasslands. Against: Kuno may be too small, leopards compete, the climate differs, and the money could protect animals already here.

check.q: Why does Mangaluru get much more rain than Bengaluru?
check.a: Mangaluru is on the sea side of the Western Ghats. Wet sea winds rise up the hills, cool and drop their rain there. Bengaluru is on the far side, in the rain shadow.
